messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am using the Dail-Madsen model as defined in AHM2, which allows to infer survival (S) and recruitment (R). The model is runs and converges in JAGS but I converted it to Nimble.
I define S and R for i sites and t years as follow:

        S[i,t+1] ~ dbin(phi[i,t], N[i,t])
        R[i, t+1] ~ dpois(gamma[i,t])

However, unlike JAGS, I obtain the following messages for both S and R:
'Warning: slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions for 'S[5, 55]'. Current parameter value is 16.'
(quite similar to this post <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/fKx8OD7Qn9s>)
Surprisingly, these messages appear only from the 2nd chain onward.

This model also correct for detection. While trying to see where the problem was coming from, I took off this detection part of the code, which is defined as follow:

            logit(p[i,t]) <- alpha.p
            C[i,t] ~ dbin(p[i,t], N[i,t])

After taking it off, the message was not appearing anymore. Thus, I am a bit confused: the messages are related to S and R but the problem seems to be caused by the detection part. Do you have any thought about the cause of the problem?

I can share a reprex if it can help.

Best,
François

messages.subject: Runtime of bootstrap filter
messages.subject_clean: Runtime of bootstrap filter
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I've been using the fantastic nimbleSMC package (thank you!) for wildlife population dynamics models and was looking at runtimes of the bootstrap filter with changing number of particles, mostly to decide on the algorithm setting when using the bootstrap filter within a PMCMC algorithm. I noticed that the runtime per particle decreases until about 1000 particles and then increases again (at least on my computer). Is there an explanation for that? And do you have a recommendation for how to factor this in when deciding on the number of particles for a PMCMC algorithm?
Thanks!

Here is a reproducible example, using the model and code from Chapter 8.1.1 of the user manual:

timeModelCode <- nimbleCode({
  x[1] ~ dnorm(mu_0, 1)
  y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], 1)
  for(i in 2:t){
    x[i] ~ dnorm(x[i-1] * a + b, 1)
    y[i] ~ dnorm(x[i] * c, 1)
  }

  a ~ dunif(0, 1)
  b ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  c ~ dnorm(1,1)
  mu_0 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
})
t <- 25; mu_0 <- 1
x <- rnorm(1 ,mu_0, 1)
y <- rnorm(1, x, 1)
a <- 0.5; b <- 1; c <- 1
for(i in 2:t){
  x[i] <- rnorm(1, x[i-1] * a + b, 1)
  y[i] <- rnorm(1, x[i] * c, 1)
}
rTimeModel <- nimbleModel(timeModelCode, constants = list(t = t),
                          data <- list(y = y), check = FALSE )
rTimeModel$a <- 0.5
rTimeModel$b <- 1
rTimeModel$c <- 1
rTimeModel$mu_0 <- 1

cTimeModel <- compileNimble(rTimeModel)
rBootF <- buildBootstrapFilter(rTimeModel, "x",
                               control = list(thresh = 0.8, saveAll = TRUE,
                                              smoothing = FALSE))
cBootF <- compileNimble(rBootF,project = rTimeModel)

n.particles <- c(3,10,30,100,300,1000,3000,10000,30000)
B <- 100

runtimes <- numeric(length(n.particles))
for(i in 1:length(n.particles)){
  print(i)
  start_time <- Sys.time()
  for(b in 1:B){
    cBootF$run(n.particles[i])
  }
  runtimes[i] <- difftime(Sys.time(), start_time, units = "secs")
}

plot((runtimes/n.particles)[2:9]*10, pch = 1, xaxt = "n", xlab = "Number of particles N",
     ylab = "ms/particle")
axis(1, at = 1:8, labels = n.particles[2:9])

I'm experiencing something new that I have no idea how to debug.

I have a model using a distribution of my own. The model compiles without problem. Then I configure an MCMC and I compile it, again without problem. But when i try to run the compiled MCMC Rstudio crashes.
The MCMC works fine in the uncompiled version and, after some testing, I found that it seems to crash before even running the first line of the first sample. I even tried creating an MCMC with only an empty sampler (i.e. doing absolutely nothing) but it still crashes...

As I have no idea what the compiled MCMC is doing before calling the samplers I'm quite lost as to what I should look into.

I could send a script generating the error if necessary.

Thanks !
Rémi

Hi,

I would like to use integration with NIMBLE (as mentioned in this post https://kenkellner.com/blog/models-with-integrals.html <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/kenkellner.com/blog/models-with-integrals.html__;!!N3hqHg43uw!p_KLI51jFGXSC3mWzBOK1GBiJtoKIBlWATLEjcv4a70q5s1Gbd9-AWhq4KAnAheCGrFKrylgB3zx8OgrigGAj2cvF_oPzg$>).

I define the function to be integrated:
R_integrator <- nimbleFunction(
   run <- function(params = double(1)){
    a <- params[1];    b <- params[2];    c <- params[3];    d <- params[4];    x <- params[5]
    integrand <- function(u,a,b,c,d,x) {
      exp(-(b/2)*((u-a)^2))/((2*d+((x-u)^2))^(c+0.5))
    }
    int_temp <-  integrate(integrand,a = a, b = b,
                           c = c, d = d, x = x, lower = -Inf, upper = Inf)[["value"]]
    int_final <- ((2*d)^c/beta(c,0.5))*sqrt(b/(2*pi))*int_temp
    returnType(double(0)) # return type declaration
    return(int_final)
  }
)
which works as expected:
R_integrator(c(2,3,4,5,-2))

and then define the model:
mod <- nimbleCode({
   mu ~ dunif(-100,100)
  sigma ~ dunif(0,20)
   z ~ dnorm(mu, pow(sigma,-2))

   params_val[1] <-1
   params_val[2] <-2
   params_val[3] <-3
   params_val[4] <-4
   params_val[5] <-z

  L<- R_integrator(params_val[1:5])
})

However, when I try to run it it states that:
"R function 'R_integrator' has arguments that cannot be evaluated; either the function must be a nimbleFunction or values for the following inputs must be specified as constants in the model"

Any help would be much appreciated.
Many Thanks,
Philip

messages.subject: Re: Integration in NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: Integration in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

The error message is a bit misleading, but at least one issue here is that the code in a nimbleFunction has to be code that the NIMBLE compiler can translate to C++.
The compiler cannot translate function() or integrate(). If you want to use an R function like integrate(), you'll need to use nimbleRcall (the link you gave illustrates this) to call out to R code from a nimbleFunction. Please see help(nimbleRcall) or the relevant section of our manual, and let us know if you have questions.

Also, at risk of raising expectations prematurely, we are planning to work to provide integration in a way that is built into NIMBLE, but that is a longer-term project we'll be working on over the next 1-3 years.

-Chris

messages.subject: Re: Runtime of bootstrap filter
messages.subject_clean: Runtime of bootstrap filter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fanny,

That's a very interesting observation.  I don't have an immediate explanation for this.  It sounds potentially system-specific, but I'm guessing.

We have a simulation exercise about PMCMC performance in the JSS paper on nimbleSMC (http://statistik-jstat.uibk.ac.at/article/view/v100i03).   The guidance that emerges is to use enough particles that the MCMC mixing doesn't get stuck due to occasionally getting stochastically very much too-large log likelihoods.  But beyond that you don't need to use so many particles that you are pursuing extremely accurate log likelihoods.  The PMCMC samples the correct posterior even though the particle filter only approximates the log likelihood.  It just needs enough particles to be sufficiently accurate to not mix terribly due to noise in the log likelihoods.  I hope that makes sense.

I will think more about your computational efficiency results and give it a try soon.  Thanks for posting this.

Perry

Hi Philip,

Also, I am just realizing that the immediate cause of the error message is that you have

run <- function

when you need

run = function

I.e., run is an argument of nimbleFunction, so it needs to be specified in the usual way that arguments are given, with '='.
As it is, your run function is actually being passed in as the first argument to nimbleFunction(), which is 'setup'.

messages.subject: Extending the MCMC chain - solved already?
messages.subject_clean: Extending the MCMC chain - solved already?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am starting a new project now and considering to use nimble; so I am checking if there is any update about the biggest nimble setback I found in my past project. Unlike in JAGS and others, it was not possible in nimble to save the model and later extend the MCMC chains of the saved model when more iterations are needed. It was only possible to extend the MCMC chain within the same R session, but once that one ended, the model is saved and later restored, it no longer worked. (So especially in parallel processing, it was virtually impossible to get the extend)

Thanks for the update!

Tomas

messages.subject_clean: Extending the MCMC chain - solved already?
messages.body_plain:
Other developers might have more to add to this - regarding the future ability to save models - but as of now: you are correct, you cannot save a model, or MCMC.  You can, however, in a new R session build an identical model and MCMC, and begin execution from exactly where the last MCMC left off - both in terms of the values of the parameters being sampled, and also the internal adaptation and tuning of the MCMC.  If you also take the extra step of saving the old R RNG seed, and restoring it to that value, this approach is equivalent (in terms of the samples generated) to having run the original chain longer.

Would that be helpful to you, for the time being?

Daniel

Hi Tomas,

Just wanted to double what Daniel wrote. In my case I save all variates as Monitor2, with a thinning equal to the number of iterations, so that only their last values are saved (or more exactly I assign to Monitor2 the variates that are not already monitored in Monitor1). These values can be used as initial values in a new chain that is set up identically to the first otherwise. In my case I do this in case I want to run the (finished) chain for longer, after checking some diagnostics.

Cheers,
Luca

messages.subject_clean: R object of different size than NimArrDouble
messages.body_plain:
Good morning everyone,
here I am,using again nible to study population trends of amphibians!

I am preparing an occupancy model to estimate trends of occupancy for some amphibian species. I realized that including spatial autocorrelation is a fundamental step, hence I added an ICAR model that estimates a spatial random effect.

The model works, but I get this warning: "Warning: R object of different size than NimArrDouble. R obj has size 1 but NimArrDbl has size 20." and I can't find a way to understand where is the error. I can just tell you that "20" is the dimension of the primary periods (years / sampling seasons).
I attach the data for one of the species and paste the script below, hoping that you can help me to discover where the error is.

All the best,
Mattia

library(nimble)

model <- nimbleCode({

  # Prior for the variance of CAR model
  psi_tau ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 10), 0, ) # Truncated normal distribution with mean 0 and SD = 10
  # Spatial effect - CAR model
  psi_rho[1:nsite] ~ dcar_normal(adj=adj[1:sumneigh],weights=weights[1:sumneigh],num=num_adj[1:nsite],tau=psi_tau, zero_mean = 1)

  # Model for occupancy
  for (k in 1:nyear){
    for (i in 1:nsite){
    logit(psi[i,k]) <- alpha + beta.trend*year[k] + eps.year[k] + psi_rho[i]
    }
    eps.year[k] ~ dnorm(0, tau.lpsi) # Year random effect
  }
  alpha <- logit(mean.psi)
  mean.psi ~ dunif(0,1)
  beta.trend ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  tau.lpsi <- pow(sd.lpsi, -2)
  sd.lpsi ~ dunif(0, 10)

  # Ecological submodel
  for (i in 1:nsite){
    for (k in 1:nyear){
      z[i,k] ~ dbern(psi[i,k])
    }
  }

  # Priors for observational model
  p_int   ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  # Observational model
  for (i in 1:nsite){
    for (k in 1:nyear){
      for (j in 1:Tf[i,k]){ # Apply only to Tf[i,k] to avoid estimation of NA surveys
        muy[i,j,k] <- z[i,k]*p[i,j,k]
        logit(p[i,j,k]) <- p_int
        y[i,j,k] ~ dbern(muy[i,j,k])
      }
    }
  }

  # Derived parameters
  for (k in 1:nyear){
    occ[k] <- sum(z[1:nsite,k]) # Occupancy in each year
  }

})

# Load data
load("dataset_occupancy.Rdata")

# Exclude NA in secondary periods
Tf <- matrix(1, nrow = dim(tab)[1], ncol = dim(tab)[3])
for (i in 1:nrow(Tf)){
  for(k in 1:ncol(Tf)){
    m <- max(which(is.na <http://is.na>(tab[i,,k]) == FALSE))

    if(m != "-Inf"){ Tf[i,k] <- m}
  }
}

# FORMATTING DATA
win.data <- list(y = tab)
constants  <- list(nsite = dim(tab)[1], nyear = dim(tab)[3],
                   year = years-mean(c(min(years),max(years))),
                   adj = adiacenti,num_adj = num_adiacenti, sumneigh = sumneigh, weights = rep(1,sumneigh))

## RUN THE MODEL
# Parameters to monitor
params <- c("alpha","beta.trend","eps.year","sd.lpsi","occ","psi.trend",
            "p_int", "psi_tau","psi_rho")

# inits
inits <-list(alpha = rnorm(1,0,1), beta.trend = rnorm(1,0,1),

             p_int = rnorm(1,0,1),
             psi_tau=runif(1,1,10),psi_rho=runif(dim(tab)[1],-1,1))

# MCMC
nc <- 3 # Numero di catene
ni <- 6*10^3 # Numero di iterazioni
nb <- ni*2/3 # Burn-in

messages.subject: Re: Issue indexing in NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: Issue indexing in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
I think that's a good suggestion.

When model code has nested indexing on the right-hand side (RHS) vs left-hand side (LHS), the situations are quite different.

On the RHS, say

y[i] <- delta[S[i]]

then S[i] might be constants, data, or a latent state.  And in any of those cases it may have duplicate entries.  If it is constants, the model relationships (which element of delta each y[i] depends on) are fixed; all steps will be faster in this case.  If it is latent state (there is a stochastic declaration with S[i] on the LHS elsewhere in the model), then we call it dynamic or stochastic indexing, and the S[i]s are sampled by MCMC (and everything will run slower, because really each y[i] depends potentially on any element of delta, so avoid this if it's not necessary).  If it is data, the S[i] won't be sampled but the computations will still be slower.  I think we warning-trap this case and suggest making the nested index (S[i]) a constant instead of data.

On the LHS, say

y[S[i]] <- delta[i]

S[i] must be constants and must have no duplicate entries.  It must be constants because we don't support stochastic dependencies that would arise if it isn't; they don't make as much sense.  There must be no duplicate entries because there can't be two declarations for the same element of y.

So another problem could be if you have S as constants but have duplicate entries.

More about the distinction between data and constants can be found in our user manual.

I hope the bit of explanation helps clarify things.

I had neglected to include S in either the constants or the data, so I added it to the list of constants. But, there is now an issue with multiple definitions for some nodes, and I don't understand the reason that is happening. Here is the full code, as I think it is more important now:

occ_code = nimbleCode({

  # First time period - no autoregression

  for (n in 1:S_n) {

    # Occupancy probability
    logit(psi[n]) <- beta_0 + inprod(beta[1:C_b], X_b[n,1:C_b]) + delta_b[S[n]]

    # Presence
    Z[n] ~ dbern(psi[n])

    # Detection probability

    logit(p[S[n]]) <- alpha_0 + delta_a[S[n]] + inprod(alpha[1:C_a], X_a[n,1:C_a])

    # Recorded
    Y[n] ~ dbern(Z[n] * p[S[n]])
  }

  # With autoregression (gamma * psi[n-S_n])
  for (n in (S_n+1):N) {

    # Occupancy probability
    logit(psi[n]) <- beta_0 + inprod(beta[1:C_b], X_b[n,1:C_b]) + delta_b[S[n]] +
      (gamma * psi[n-S_n])

    # Presence
    Z[n] ~ dbern(psi[n])

    # Detection probability

    logit(p[S[n]]) <- alpha_0 + delta_a[S[n]] + inprod(alpha[1:C_a], X_a[n,1:C_a])

    # Recorded
    Y[n] ~ dbern(Z[n] * p[S[n]])
  }

  # Priors
  for (c in 1:C_b) {
    beta[c] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
  }
  beta_0 ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)

  for (c in 1:C_a) {
    alpha[c] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
  }
  alpha_0 ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)

  for (s in 1:S_n) {
    delta_b[s] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
    delta_a[s] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
  }

  gamma ~ T(dnorm(0, 0.01), 0, 1)
})

messages.body_plain:
It looks like in

for (n in 1:S_n)

you have declarations for p[1]...p[242]
and then in

for (n in (S_n+1):N)

you again have declarations for p[1]...p[242]

That would be duplicate declarations.  I'm not sure if there is a confusion about how the model language works or just a coding confusion.  The model language is a declarative language.  That means it doesn't matter in what order declarations appear.  The declarations are putting together a graphical model.  It is not allowed to declare the same node twice.  I am wondering if you want p[n] instead of p[S[n]].

Perry

> > > On the RHS, say

Hi Perry,
thank you very much.
Indeed, it was the prior of eps.year and by correcting its dimension the warning disappeared.

I have another question on the same model, maybe less nimble-related.
I made two versions of the model, one simple and one with spatial autocorrelation. No problem at all with the simple model, however, with the one including a spatial effect, I can't get the right plot for the population trend.
I attach here an example: in the first case both number of occupied sites (blue dots) and the trend (black line with grey posteriors) are fine; in the second case, occupied sites are correct, but I the plot of the trend is clearly wrong:

Here is the script, consider that the first part is an update of the previos script. I attach an Rdata to make it possible to run the script just from the "PLOT" section:

library(nimble)

model <- nimbleCode({

  # Prior for the variance of CAR model
  psi_tau ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 10), 0, ) # Truncated normal distribution with mean 0 and SD = 10
  # Spatial effect - CAR model
  psi_rho[1:nsite] ~ dcar_normal(adj=adj[1:sumneigh],weights=weights[1:sumneigh],num=num_adj[1:nsite],tau=psi_tau, zero_mean = 1)

  # Model for occupancy
  for (k in 1:nyear){
    for (i in 1:nsite){
      logit(psi[i,k]) <- alpha + beta.trend*year[k] + eps.year[k] + psi_rho[i]
    }
    eps.year[k] ~ dnorm(0, tau.lpsi) # Year random effect
  }
  alpha <- logit(mean.psi)
  mean.psi ~ dunif(0,1)
  beta.trend ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  tau.lpsi <- pow(sd.lpsi, -2)
  sd.lpsi ~ dunif(0, 10)

  # Ecological submodel
  for (i in 1:nsite){
    for (k in 1:nyear){
      z[i,k] ~ dbern(psi[i,k])
    }
  }

  # Priors for observational model
  p_int   ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
  # Observational model
  for (i in 1:nsite){
    for (k in 1:nyear){
      for (j in 1:Tf[i,k]){ # Apply only to Tf[i,k] to avoid estimation of NA surveys
        muy[i,j,k] <- z[i,k]*p[i,j,k]
        logit(p[i,j,k]) <- p_int

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mattia,

I guess we'd have to see the model code including the spatial model (which might be centered or not) to try to see what's going on.  But first I'd suggest exploring the compiled model object itself to be sure you are seeing all the contributions you need for the post-hoc predictions you are calculating.  For example, after running the MCMC, the last state of the chain will still be in the compiled model.  You can then look at its values, e.g.
Cmodel$eps.year
etc.
This should allow you to probe whether you are reconstructing the calculations correctly.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry, thank you for the very useful suggestion.
In the end, I managed to understand the error in calculation, I explain it below for completeness.

What I wanted was a line indicating the estimated trend of occupied sites without the year random effect.
Mark Kery's model, that I used as a base, calculated this as a derived parameter:

 for (k in 1:nyear){

    logit(psi.trend[k]) <- alpha + beta.trend*year[k]
  }

In my model I added spatial autocorrelation and I was wrongly supposing that since the average of the spatial model was 0, I could exclude it from calculations.
Instead, the correct calculation needs an additional step:

  for (k in 1:nyear){

    for(i in 1:nsite){
      logit(psi.site[i,k]) <- alpha + beta.trend*year[k] + psi_rho[i] # The last one is the spatial term
    }
   psi.trend[k] <- sum(psi.site[1:nsite,k])
  }

Thank you for your support!
Mattia

In the model, 'scale' has a value of NA and causes NA values for mu and the message you saw.  It is useful to check using model$calculate(nodes) when you get NA/NaN issues to see which nodes caused the issue. This makes error tracking easier. Hope it helps.

Best wishes,
Wei

messages.subject_clean: Nimble package running too slow
messages.body_plain:
Dear Suzy,

I took a relatively brief look at your code.  It looks like you have 526*526 data points.  You have 526 multivariate normals, each of length 526, so each with a covariance matrix that is 526x526.  You are setting each of the covariance matrices to a diagonal matrix, so all covariances are 0.  Using dmnorm like this will force a costly matrix computation (including a Cholesky decomposition followed by a matrix multiplication or a solve) for every MCMC update of every parameter (and you have 12*526 coefficients).  If this is a toy working towards a case where you need non-zero covariances, then the answer might simply be that these are indeed costly computations for a large model.  But if this is really what you want, it would be better to use univariate normals and avoid the costly matrix computations.  Also, I'm not immediately following your model.  I've more often seen something like psi_y[i] * exp(-Dist[1:N, 1:N]/lambda) to calculate a covariance matrix.  You are using diag(psi_y[i] * exp(-Dist[1:N, i]/lambda)) to calculate each of i separate precision matrices.  Again, I might not be seeing it.  Often people provide some explanation of their model when posting to this list.  If you need greater clarity on what your model code is creating, I'd suggest not using nimbleMCMC and instead building the model yourself using nimbleModel and exploring its calculations using model$calculate etc.  HTH.

Perry

messages.subject: specifying different data for first iteration only?
messages.subject_clean: specifying different data for first iteration only?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working with an age-structured Jolly-Seber model (superpopulation
parameterization with data augmentation.) Ages are observed without error for
real individuals. The time 1 population is comprised of individuals of many ages.
Entries in time 2 and beyond are by birth only. For augmented individuals, I
would like to initialize all ages at “NA” so the ages can simply be determined by
the code.

That works fine if survival and recapture rates are not age-specific.
However, if rates are age-specific, then the initialization fails because there
is an “NA” being used as an index. For example, any individual in time t has a
survival rate of phi[t, NA].

I am able to work around this by assigning all augmented
individuals an age in time 1. But that means I need many groups of augmented
individuals—e.g., if there are 10 ages, there need to be 11 groups of augmented
individuals (the extra group is for not yet born). And all groups of augmented
individuals have to be pretty large, so I end up with a much larger augmented population
and run time than I would like.

Is there a way I can do something different on the first
iteration to get around the initialization problem? Perhaps assign everyone a non-age-dependent
survival rate on the first iteration only? Or assign everyone an initial age in
the first time period for the first iteration, but then let those initial ages
be overwritten in subsequent iterations?

I hope this makes sense. I’ll copy code below. Thank you!!

Rebecca

code <- nimbleCode({
  psi ~ dbeta(1,1)  # psi = inclusion parameter (is individual real or fake)
  for (t in 1:K){
    for(aa in 1:max.age){   # age 0 means not yet born
      p[t,aa+1] ~ dbeta(1,1)# p[t,aa+1] = cap rate for time t, age aa; age 0 cap rate = 0
    }
  }
  for (t in 1:(K-1)){
    for(aa in 1:(max.age-1)){
      phi[t,aa+1] ~ dbeta(1,1) # phi[t,aa+1] = surv rate for time t, age aa; age 0 surv rate = 0
    }
  }
  beta[1:K] ~ ddirch(b[1:K])   # betas = unconditional entry probabilities
  eta[1] <- beta[1]            # etas = corresponding conditional probabilities
  for(k in 2:K){eta[k] <- beta[k]/(1-sum(beta[1:(k-1)]))}

  # piAGE = age distribution of animals alive in the population at time 1
  # piAGEuncond has an additional "age 0" which means "not yet born".
  # Entries after time 1 are by birth only
  piAGE[1:max.age] ~ ddirch(a[1:max.age])
  piAGEuncond[1:(max.age+1)] <- c( (1-eta[1]), eta[1]*piAGE[1:max.age] )

  # Likelihoods
  for (i in 1:M){    # M = size of augmented population
    w[i] ~ dbern(psi)# w[i] = indicator if individual i is real

    # agePlusOne are time 1 age data + 1
    agePlusOne[i] ~ dcat(piAGEuncond[1:(max.age+1)])
    age[i,1] <- (agePlusOne[i]-1)

    # state process
    u[i,1] <- step(age[i,1]-.1)  # u[i,j] = indicator for alive
    z[i,1] <- u[i,1]*w[i]

    # Observation process
    yprob_t1[i,1] <- z[i,1]*p[1,age[i,1]+1]
    y[i,1] ~ dbern(yprob_t1[i,1] )

    # avail[i,j] = indicator if not yet recruited from superpop to pop
    avail[i,1] <- 1 - u[i,1]

    for (t in 2:K){
      # State process
      uprob[i,t] <- u[i,t-1]*phi[t-1,age[i,t-1]+1]  + avail[i,t-1]*eta[t]
      u[i,t] ~ dbern(uprob[i,t])
      z[i,t] <- u[i,t]*w[i]

      # Age process: grows older by one year after recruitment
      age[i,t] <- age[i,t-1] + max(u[i,1:t])

      # Observation process
      yprob[i,t] <- z[i,t]*p[t,age[i,t]+1]
      y[i,t] ~ dbern(yprob[i,t])

      # avail[i,j] = indicator if not yet recruited from superpop to pop
      avail[i,t] <- 1- max(u[i,1:t])
    } #t
  } #i
})#END model

messages.body_plain:
A few years ago, Richard Chandler posted a little trick on the HMEcology listserv that basically suggested that you could set spatial CMR likelihoods up in a way that only used the pseudo-individuals to inform the state process and completely exclude them from the observation process. This idea was expanded on by Alexandra Curtis to Jolly-Seber population models. I have no idea if this has entered the vetted ecological literature, but I messed around with the idea a bit, and it seemed pretty sound. So,although this doesn't change the number of pseudo-individuals you are using, it does change the extent to which they can bog down your model.

I am just going to include an example code that I have used in the past that should be relatively similar to your code. I think this example was specifically written for JAGS, but I am not immediately seeing any nimble red flags.

    ######################################
    # State Process
    ######################################
    for (i in 1:M){                                                   # Loop through real + psuedo individuals
     w[i] ~ dbern(psi)                                               # Latent inclusion state
     z[i,1] ~ dbern(eta[1])                                         # Entry into first occasion

    for (t in 2:n.occasions) {
      q[i,t-1] <- 1 - z[i,t-1]                                                 # Have not entered yet
      mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1] + eta[t] * prod(q[i,1:(t-1)]) # Presence = survived since last + entered since last
      z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
    }
    }

    ######################################
    # Observation Process
    ######################################
    for (i in 1:n.ch <http://n.ch>){                            # Loop through real individuals
      y[i,1] ~ dbern(z[i,1] * p[1] * w[i])     # Latent state * detection * latent inclusion
    for (t in 2:n.occasions){
     y[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t] * p[t] * w[i])        # Latent state * detection * latent inclusion
    }
    }

    ######################################
    # Chandler trick
    ######################################
    for(i in (n.ch <http://n.ch>+1):M) {                                        # Loop through psuedo individuals
      pzo[i,1] <- 1 - (p[1] * z[i,1] * w[i])                      # probability of not being detected on first occasion
    for (t in 2:n.occasions){
      pzo[i,t] <- 1 - (p[t] * z[i,t] * w[i])                         # probability of not being detected on each other occasion
    }
      zeros[i] ~ dbern(1-prod(pzo[i,]))                         # probability of at being detected at least once (zeros = vector of 0's for each augmented individual)
    }

#################
 This last bold-italicized part is the time saver. Instead of doing a bernoulli trial for i * t for these imaginary individuals, you just do it once for each psuedo-individual based on the probability of it being detected once per the duration of the study.

-Dan

Dan,

Thanks for that trick--it looks like it could be very useful for me down the road!  But I don't think it takes care of my current problem.

Since my current model is age-structured, I need to pull out survival rates as phi[t, age] and recap rates as p[t, age]. But if age is specified as NA in the first time period (for the augmented individuals), I get an index-out-of-bounds error. If I specify a numeric age in the first time period for an augmented individual, then I don't think its age can't be overwritten in subsequent iterations. Thus, if K is the maximum age, I need K+1 separate groups of augmented individuals.

Is there something I can do to separate out the first iteration to fix this? Perhaps assign everyone a non-age-dependent survival rate on the first iteration only? Or assign everyone an initial age in the first time period for the first iteration, but then let those initial ages be overwritten in subsequent iterations?

Thanks!

Rebecca

messages.body_plain:
Hello to all,

I'm new to this group and to Nimble.  I've already run a few models without any problems but I'm aiming at a binomial logistic regression. Whatever the number of variables I use and whatever their transformation and initial values the model does not work and returns "logProb is -Inf". In the MCMC chains the values do not mix. The null model (only with alpha) seems to work. I think it could be a numerical problem.  I propose here an example associated with a small representative data set (sample_n(1000) on 50k):

small_data <- readRDS("small_data.rds")

library(nimble, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

Nb_iter = 1000
Nb_chains = 4
Nb_burnin = 10
Nb_thin = 1

code <- nimbleCode({

  alpha ~ dnorm(0, 100)
  beta_Nb_obs ~ dnorm(0, 100)
  #beta_weather_1~ dnorm(0, 100)

  #likelihood

  for(i in 1:N){
    success[i] ~ dbern(P[i])
    logit(P[i])  <- alpha +
      beta_Nb_obs*Nb_obs[i] #+
      #beta_weather_1*weather_1[i]
  }
})

constants <- list(N = nrow(small_data),
                  Nb_obs = small_data$Nb_obs#,
                  #weather_1 = small_data$weather_1
)

data <- list(success = as.integer(as.character(small_data$success)))

N = nrow(small_data)
my_rnorm <- function(n) rnorm(n,0,100)
inits <- function() {
  list(alpha = my_rnorm(1),
       beta_Nb_obs = my_rnorm(1)#,
       #beta_weather_1 = my_rnorm(1),
       #P = runif(N, min = 0.01, max = 0.99)
  )
}

model <- nimbleModel(code, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits())

conf <- configureMCMC(model)

CsimMCMC <- compileNimble(model)

simMCMC <- buildMCMC(conf)

last_compil <- compileNimble(simMCMC, project = CsimMCMC)

samples <- runMCMC(last_compil, niter = Nb_iter, nchains = Nb_chains, nburnin = Nb_burnin, thin = Nb_thin)

The idea is to eventually run this model:

logit(P[i]) <- alpha + Nb_obs[i] +
  beta_weather_1*weather_1[i] +
  beta_weather_2*weather_2[i] +
  beta_weather_3*weather_3[i] +
  beta_weather_4*weather_4[i] +
  beta_month[month[i]] +
  beta_group[group[i]] +

messages.body_plain:
Pablo,
Thanks for posting and providing the reproducible example.
It looks like your initial values indeed give impossible relationships in the model.  Specifically, there are many instances with P == 1 and success == 0, so that the log probability of the success value is log(0), which is -Inf.
Here is how I've inspected your model (following nimbleModel):

model$calculate() # returns -Inf, as you've seen when you run an MCMC.
model$alpha         # shows  your inits value for alpha
model$beta_Nb_obs.    # shows your inits value for beta_Nb_obs
sum(model$P == 1)       # For the inits values I got from your code, all values of P are numerically *exactly* 1.
summary(constants$Nb_obs) # I see that your covariate is not centered and ranges from 3 to 55, so potentially small values of beta_Nb_obs can result in some or all P numerically exactly 1 (or possibly numerically exactly 0 for other random inits values of model$alpha and/or model$beta_Nb_obs).
sum(model$success == 0) # 596 values of success have value 0
which(model$success == 0)[1]  # Let's find the first case where success is a 0.  It is the first element.
model$calculate("success[1]").  # Let's see that the log probability of the first datum is -Inf, because it is impossible for dbern with prob == 1 to give a 0.
model$P[1]            # Here is the probability for dbern, exactly 1
model$success[1] # Here is the  corresponding datum, which is 0
dbinom(0, 1, 1, log = TRUE)  # Your model is doing this calculation internally, which returns -Inf
model$alpha <- rnorm(1, 0, .1).  # If you choose initial values of much smaller magnitude, something like rnorm(1, 0, .1)
model$beta_Nb_obs <- rnorm(1, 0, .1).  # and here as well
model$calculate()  # the model now gives a valid log likelihood

When initial values make the model invalid from the start, sometimes the MCMC can recover, but often it can't.  It's important to check your initial values and ensure that the model makes sense with them.

HTH
Perry

Dear Pablo,
I had tried rnorm(1, 0, 1) before trying rnorm(1, 0, .1).  What I saw with rnorm(1, 0, 1) was that I could still often get initial value draws for the parameters that were large enough to generate elements of model$P that were numerically exactly 0 or 1, due to the large values in your covariate.  You may wish to standardize (center and scale) your covariate, but otherwise you will need to provide initial values of your parameters on appropriate scales.  The inits are randomly drawn, so you could on one run have it "work" and on another run not. If you reduce the sd of the inits distribution sufficiently, then it should work nearly all the time.  I am not sure what would be making entries of model$P be NA, except that if you have run the MCMC for some iterations, the presence of a log prob that is -Inf somewhere in the model can result in invalid values propagating throughout the model.  It is likely that initial values are the problem and that you need to reduce further the scale of your random draws.  You should not need to run MCMC to see if there is a problem. You should be able to do model$calculate() immediately after nimbleModel(...) and see if you get a valid result (a number rather than NA, -Inf, or NaN).  If you get a number, you should be able to proceed to running MCMC.
Best wishes,
Perry

The response variable is a matrix of j columns and 4 rows, where a column is either 0100, or 0010, etc. OR NA for all 4 rows.
I’d like the missing columns to be filled in as 0010 or 0100 etc. with equal probability of a 1 in each column, but I don’t want to affect the actual data, which has a different (non random) distribution of ones.
Is there a way to simulate data for the missing values at each iteration and just pass them along as data into the model?

I'm struggling with 2 problems
1) how to simulate the data I want in nimble

is it y[1:4,j]~dcat(c(0.25,0.25,0,25,0,25)) for the missing records?

And 2) if so how do I integrate those values into the actual model? ie how do I get them back on the left side of the equation without ending up with a double assignment to those values?

thanks for any advice,

Robin R.

Hi Nimble experts,

I am trying to fit a locally smooth model, and I am wondering if this can be achieved in Nimble. The general idea of this model is to allow a large jump in the true values between adjacent areal units. Please see the attached picture for model description. Specifically, I am not sure if nimble allows the uniform prior has (-inf, inf). Thanks in advance!

The beta is a piecewise constant intercept that allows sudden jumps in the spatial surface between adjacent units. This constant intercept term has q distinct values, and if adjacent units are in different groups, their probability may have different values. Additionally, the number 1 before the semi-colon in the multinomial model indicates there is only 'one' trail in the multinomial distribution, as each areal unit can only have one intercept term. I am also wondering if the multinomial prior can be achieved under Nimble.

messages.body_plain:
Alex, some quick thoughts on this, although I don't believe I'm fully grasping your model:

A Uniform prior with support on (-Inf, Inf), can be achieved using the dflat() prior distribution.

That said, the Uniform prior specification for your beta_i coefficients, each of which depends on beta_{I+1} and beta_{i-1}, would cause a cyclic graph definition, which is not allowed in NIMBLE.  There may be other ways to achieve what you're trying to do here, mathematically identical, perhaps with a multivariate specification of the full beta vector.

Yes, the multinomial prior can be used in NIMBLE, that won't pose a problem.  If your multinomial has 1 trial, I'll point out that's equivalent to using a categorical prior (dcat), which will be sampled in a fundamentally different way, and I suspect would improve the overall mixing of your model.

Others may have more helpful advice for you, but these were my quick thoughts.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rebecca,

Thanks for this.  And thanks for the suggestion, Dan.

I'm not easily grasping exactly what you need or what the problem is.  Could you try to pinpoint it more clearly (possibly referring to each line of code involved)?  One thing I'm not sure about is whether your code shows your workaround or shows what you would like to have work but doesn't work.

If you need ages of augmented individuals to be latent states with valid initial values, would it work to provide their data entries as NA and their inits entries as valid values?  That is the usual approach.

You might be saying that when w[i] is sampled to be a 1 (turning "on" an augmented individual), then you want an appropriate draw for the age.  It looks like the ages are stochastic.  Can you spell it out more?  I'm not sure whether you are seeing the error at (what we call) initialization, i.e. before the first MCMC iteration, or when a w[i] is sampled (or proposed by a sampler) to be a 1.

A general comment: Data augmentation like this is a setup for inefficient MCMC.  That's because the MCMC will sample dimensions of the model relevant to augmented individuals even when they are not "in the model" (w[i] == 0).  An alternative is reversible jump MCMC customized to this kind of model.  We've experimented with that in simpler cases and it didn't help a lot, but it could help in other cases and just hasn't been something we've had time to do more with.  There are other ideas for sampling these kinds of models more effectively.  But anyway that's a side comment and does not address your problem.

Perry

> A few years ago, Richard Chandler posted a little trick on the HMEcology listserv that basically suggested that you could set spatial CMR likelihoods up in a way that only used the pseudo-individuals to inform the state process and completely exclude them from the observation process. This idea was expanded on by Alexandra Curtis to Jolly-Seber population models. I have no idea if this has entered the vetted ecological literature, but I messed around with the idea a bit, and it seemed pretty sound. So,although this doesn't change the number of pseudo-individuals you are using, it does change the extent to which they can bog down your model.
>
> I am just going to include an example code that I have used in the past that should be relatively similar to your code. I think this example was specifically written for JAGS, but I am not immediately seeing any nimble red flags.
>
>     ######################################
>     # State Process
>     ######################################
>     for (i in 1:M){                                                   # Loop through real + psuedo individuals
>      w[i] ~ dbern(psi)                                               # Latent inclusion state

>       z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
>     }
>     }

>     ######################################

>       y[i,1] ~ dbern(z[i,1] * p[1] * w[i])     # Latent state * detection * latent inclusion
>     for (t in 2:n.occasions){

messages.body_plain:
Dear Robin,
Thanks for the question.
Can you please explain a little bit more?  Is it that one and only one of the four numbers in a column should be a 1?  Or is it that each of the four numbers can be a 0 or a 1, so there could be anywhere from no 1s to four 1s?  And can you say more about what you mean by "get them back on the left side of the equation" and "just pass them along as data into the model"?  By the first phrase, do you mean you want them to follow one distribution for purposes of imputing missing data but another distribution in other model calculations?  Often, but not always, when that situation arises there is a glitch in the probability reasoning and one needs to re-think the model.  If it is really what you want, there are tricks to get two log probability contributions out of one node in the model.  But it would help if you can explain more.  By the second phrase, do you mean you want the values imputed *once* and then used as data, meaning they are not changing? I don't think that's what you mean, but that is normally what we mean by a "data" node in a model.  A node with "missing data" is a latent state (if there are other data nodes that eventually depend on it) or a posterior predictive node, but in either case we don't refer to it as a "data" node.  So I just want to be sure I understand what you mean before diving into solution ideas.
Perry

Hi All,

I have a query about using nimbleList data structures as outputs for nimbleFunctions (which are included in model code). Based on the examples in Chapter 14 I wrote the following toy nimbleFunction:

mynf <- nimbleFunction(
  setup = function(){
    my_List_Def <- nimbleList(ouput1 = double(1), ouput2 = double(2))
  },
  run = function(input1 = double(1), input2 = double(2)){

    output_List <- my_List_Def$new()
    output_List$ouput1 <- input1
    output_List$ouput2 <- input2

    returnType(my_List_Def())
    return(output_List)
  }
)
Presumably because I have specified the "setup" argument I need to assign it to another object and then supply the arguments using $run(...) to get the required output?

mynf2 <- mynf()
mynf2$run(c(1,2), diag(2))

I'm not sure if this is the correct way to do it and furthermore how do I use this function in the model code?

Can I specify a nimbleList within the model code?

Many Thanks,
Philip

Dear Philip,

It is not currently possible to return a nimbleList in model code, or to use a nimbleFunction with setup code in model code.

One solution could be to use numeric objects (vectors, matrices, arrays) as data structures following a protocol that you use consistently.  E.g. if you need to keep input1 and input2 packed into a data structure together, you could make it a matrix with two columns.  If the sizes of relevant values need to change over the course of using the model, you would need the matrix that holds them to take the maximal possible size.  If you have other user-defined functions that need to use them and determine what the lengths of relevant values are, you could either hold the lengths in another model variable or you could encode the end of the relevant values in each column with -1 or some such value.  I hope that makes some sense.

If those ideas don't get you moving in a useful direction, feel free to explain more of what you need.

HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,

I'll add some thoughts to Daniel's suggestions:

1) Following Daniel's comment about the betas, the difficulty here is specifying the joint distribution either directly as a joint distribution or as the product of a marginal and various conditional
distributions, without having any cycles. Alternatively, you might be able to specify the beta_i values as being independent of each other and use our `dconstraint` mechanism to impose the monotonicity constraints you want. Another option would be to put your prior on the differences in the betas. I.e., you could have a prior for beta1 that has fixed constants as parameters and have beta2 = beta1 + delta1, beta3 = beta2 + delta2, etc., with the priors put on the deltas (and enforcing that each delta must be non-negative). This is appealing in terms of model specification but it might lead to slow inference because a given observation can depend on many of the deltas because of the dependency structure that such a specification produces.

2) Your specification for phi looks like a CAR prior. Is that right? We do provide both proper and improper CAR distributions in NIMBLE.

chris

On Wed, Oct 19, 2022 at 3:53 AM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:

> Alex, some quick thoughts on this, although I don't believe I'm fully grasping your model:
>
> A Uniform prior with support on (-Inf, Inf), can be achieved using the dflat() prior distribution.
>
> That said, the Uniform prior specification for your beta_i coefficients, each of which depends on beta_{I+1} and beta_{i-1}, would cause a cyclic graph definition, which is not allowed in NIMBLE. > Yes, the multinomial prior can be used in NIMBLE, that won't pose a problem.  If your multinomial has 1 trial, I'll point out that's equivalent to using a categorical prior (dcat), which will be sampled in a fundamentally different way, and I suspect would improve the overall mixing of your model.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

You can test the function and its compilation outside of a model.  I am guessing sd_diag was supposed to be sd_vec, so I've made that change.

sd_vec <- c(.2,0.5,0.1)
cov_mat <-diag(sd_vec)%*%R%*%diag(sd_vec)

mu_vec <- c(5, 2,1)
mu_condit_val <- 3

conditional_MNV(mu_vec, cov_mat, mu_condit_val) # uncompiled: works

C_conditional_MNV <- compileNimble(conditional_MNV) # compile it
C_conditional_MNV(mu_vec, cov_mat, mu_condit_val) # compiled: works

So the problem is how you are using it in a model.

Unfortunately a friction point in nimble is that compilation supports true scalars, but R does not have true scalars (only length 1 vectors).  As a result, the single value mu_condit_val[1:1] is not passed as a vector successfully.  If you will always have a scalar here, declare it as double(0) instead of double(1).  Alternatively, if sometimes you. need a vector, you can pad it with an extra 0, which you can then not use within the conditional_MVN function.

Also I would suggest a different strategy within conditional_MVN if computational efficiency is a concern.  Instead of repeating the step

cov_mat[1:index_end,(index_end+1):mat_size]%*%inverse(cov_mat[(index_end+1):mat_size,(index_end+1):mat_size])

you could do that once and re-use the result in both places where it's needed.
Another strategy would be to do this calculation within the model (or as a separate user-defined function) and then have separate functions to obtain the conditional mean and conditional covariance, using this shared part of the calculation as input.

HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Thank you for your time in advance.
I have quite a complex model that has mixing problems. Chain 2 is getting stuck in extreme values producing strange results.
In the model there is a time-dependent 6x6 transition matrix, where the first row is as follows:
    {S0[1, t], S0[2, t], S0[3, t], S0[4, t], S0[5, t], 0} # transition probability from state 1 to 1:6
in here:
    S0[1:5, t]  ~ ddirch(D_Alpha[1:5, t]) # prior
  D_Alpha[1:5, t]<-c(1/5, 1/5, 1/5, 1/5, 1/5)

I examined the correlation of the samples for each chain and found that 2 variables are highly correlated over time.
To be more specific, for chain two:
    cor(S0[3,t=16], S0[5,t=16]) =-0.993

The picture below presents a plot of the correlation matrix at different time points, each plot represents a chain 1 to 3 (left to right)
Since NIMBLE recognizes a Dirichlet distribution, it assigns a RW_dirichlet sampler to all the S0 variables.

is it possible to block this sampling in order to reduce the correlation? I try to remove the sampler and add a "RW_block" for each time point but does not seem to sample since the outcome has 0 variability.
If not, how else can I reduce this strong correlation?

Thank you for your time, any comments or ideas will be very helpful.
--
Diego

Hi Perry,

Thank you for your response and for all you do to help us.

The error was indeed on initialization, and the first line to cause the error was

yprob_t1[i,1] <- z[i,1]*p[1,age[i,1]+1] because age[i,1]equaled “NA” for the augmented individuals, making the index evaluate to [1,NA+1]. At the time I posted my question, the code only worked if time 1 age data were specified numerically for all individuals, including the augmented individuals.

I previously tried providing numerical inits for all of the entries where I wanted to have “NA” data values, but it did not work. However, since you suggested it again, I tried it again, and this time it did work—which means something else was wrong the last time I tried it. I am taking the next online course y’all are offering, so hopefully that will help me become less reliant on this forum.

I see what you are saying about inefficient sampling for this kind of data augmentation—thank you for taking the extra time to mention this! On my to-do list is combining w with the betas, which I think will alleviate the particular problem you are referencing (although please correct me if I am missing something). Next is marginalizing over individuals so I am looping through unique capture histories, not unique individuals. After that is deciding if I need to abandon data augmentation. As you can tell, however, I am taking baby steps….but if there are any written resources you can direct me to for making this more efficient, that would be outstanding.

Thank you again.

Rebecca

Subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] Re: specifying different data for first iteration only?

Hi Rebecca,

Thanks for this.  And thanks for the suggestion, Dan.

I'm not easily grasping exactly what you need or what the problem is.  Could you try to pinpoint it more clearly (possibly referring to each line of code involved)?  One thing I'm not sure about is whether your code shows your workaround or shows what you would like to have work but doesn't work.

If you need ages of augmented individuals to be latent states with valid initial values, would it work to provide their data entries as NA and their inits entries as valid values?  That is the usual approach.

You might be saying that when w[i] is sampled to be a 1 (turning "on" an augmented individual), then you want an appropriate draw for the age.  It looks like the ages are stochastic.  Can you spell it out more?  I'm not sure whether you are seeing the error at (what we call) initialization, i.e. before the first MCMC iteration, or when a w[i] is sampled (or proposed by a sampler) to be a 1.

A general comment: Data augmentation like this is a setup for inefficient MCMC.  That's because the MCMC will sample dimensions of the model relevant to augmented individuals even when they are not "in the model" (w[i] == 0).  An alternative is reversible jump MCMC customized to this kind of model.  We've experimented with that in simpler cases and it didn't help a lot, but it could help in other cases and just hasn't been something we've had time to do more with.  There are other ideas for sampling these kinds of models more effectively.  But anyway that's a side comment and does not address your problem.

Perry

This idea was expanded on by Alexandra Curtis to Jolly-Seber population models. I have no idea if this has entered the vetted ecological literature, but I messed around with the idea a bit, and it seemed pretty sound. So,although this doesn't change the number of pseudo-individuals you are using, it does change the extent to which they can bog down your model.
>
> I am just going to include an example code that I have used in the past that should be relatively similar to your code. I think this example was specifically written for JAGS, but I am not immediately seeing any nimble red flags.
>
>     ######################################
>     # State Process

>     for (i in 1:M){                                                   # Loop through real + psuedo individuals
>      w[i] ~ dbern(psi)                                               # Latent inclusion state

>       z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
>     }
>     }

>       y[i,1] ~ dbern(z[i,1] * p[1] * w[i])     # Latent state * detection * latent inclusion
>     for (t in 2:n.occasions){

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I think your problem is due to the fact that the one of the taub matrices you provide to the model is not positive definite. From the way you generated the initial values for taub matrices, they cannot be guaranteed to be symmetric, which is required as a positive definite matrix. The support of the Wishart distribution consists of positive definite matrices. The non-pos-def matrix is then provided to the mv normal as a precision matrix, which is not valid. Then doing cholesky decomposition gives you the error message. Hope this helps.

Best wishes,
Wei

messages.body_plain:
Dave, the error is coming from the cyclic dependence between elements of m[] and r[], in the following code (I've combined the two for-loops into a single loop, for clarity):

    # Multinomial likelihood
    for (t in 1:(2 * (nyears - 1))){
        m[t, 1:nyears] ~ dmulti(pr[t, 1:10], r[t])
    # Calculate the number of released individuals

        r[t] <- sum(m[t, 1:10])
    }

Here, m[t, 1:nyears] depends on r[t].
And r[t] is calculated as the sum of m[t, 1:10]
This creates a cycle in the graph (r depends on m, m depends on r), which is not allowed in model code.  The code must represent a directed acyclic graph.

Right now I won't posit other modelling approaches, but hopefully others on the list might chime in with some ideas, for this multinomial observation / multinomial number of trials cyclic problem.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Thanks for Nimble - it looks like a really flexible tool.

I am learning Nimble by experimenting with implementing the "Latent Slice Sampler" of Li and Walker (2010.08509.pdf (arxiv.org) <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.08509.pdf>), specifically the very simple algorithm described in their paper's section 5 (Discussion).

I have code that seems to work on my baby test example, and runs (SLOWLY) in uncompiled form. However, when I try to compile it I get the following error:
Error in thisKeywordInfo$processor(code, nfProc) :
  object 'callerCode' not found

I read in the group that this may have something to do with runtime indexing by string, but I hacked together my sampler code from the Nimble's source for it's slice and block_RW samplers, and don't think I'm doing anything that's not done there. Any help would be appreciated. Here is the full code:

sampler_latent_slice <- nimbleFunction(
  name = 'sampler_latent_slice',
  contains = sampler_BASE,
  setup = function(model, mvSaved, target, control) {
    ## control list extraction
    scaleInit <- extractControlElement(control,'scaleInit',1)
    lambda <- extractControlElement(control,'lambda',0.1)
    tryMax <- extractControlElement(control,'tryMax',1000)

    ## node list generation
    targetAsScalar <- model$expandNodeNames(target, returnScalarComponents = TRUE,)

    calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
    calcNodesNoSelf <- model$getDependencies(target, self = FALSE)
    isStochCalcNodesNoSelf <- model$isStoch(calcNodesNoSelf)   ## should be made faster
    calcNodesNoSelfDeterm <- calcNodesNoSelf[!isStochCalcNodesNoSelf]
    calcNodesNoSelfStoch <- calcNodesNoSelf[isStochCalcNodesNoSelf]

    # store dimension of targets
    targetDimension <- length(targetAsScalar)
    cat("targetDimension ", targetDimension,"\n")

    sPrev <- rep(scaleInit,targetDimension)
    timesRan <- 0
    tries <- 0

    cat("done lss setup\n")
  },
  run = function() {
    ### Li/Walker Step 1

    u <- exp(model$getLogProb(calcNodes))
    w <- u*runif(1,min=0,max=1)
    y0 <- values(model,targetAsScalar) # I hope this works!
    l <- runif(n=targetDimension,min=y0-sPrev/2,y0+sPrev/2)
    # hope this is persisted!
    sPrev <<- rexp(n=targetDimension, rate=lambda*sPrev)+ 2*abs(l-y0) # truncated exponential - to sample we just shift by the truncation threshold

    ## Li/Walker Step 2
    a <- l - sPrev/2
    b <- l + sPrev/2

    ## Li/Walker Step 3/4
    y_star <- runif(targetDimension,min=a, max=b)
    tries <<- 1
    #  EVALUATE MODEL AT y_star
    lp <- setAndCalculateTarget(y_star)
    while( !is.nan(lp) & (exp(lp) <w)  & (tries < tryMax) ){
      for(j in 1:targetDimension){
        if( y_star[[j]] < y0[[j]]){
          a[[j]] <- max(a[[j]],y_star[[j]])
        } else {
          b[[j]] <- min(b[[j]],y_star[[j]])
        }
      }
      y_star <- runif(targetDimension,min=a, max=b)
      tries <<- tries+1
      lp <- setAndCalculateTarget(y_star)

    }

    if(tries == tryMax){
      cat("Warning: latent slice sampler reached maximum number of contractions ", tryMax,"\n")
      nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = target, logProb = TRUE) # sk test
      nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesNoSelfDeterm, logProb = FALSE)
      nimCopy(from = mvSaved, to = model, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesNoSelfStoch, logProbOnly = TRUE)

    } else {  # accept y_star
      nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = target, logProb = TRUE) # sk test
      nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesNoSelfDeterm, logProb = FALSE)
      nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, row = 1, nodes = calcNodesNoSelfStoch, logProbOnly = TRUE)

    }

  },
  methods = list(
    setAndCalculateTarget = function(valueVec = double(1)) {
      values(model,target) <<- valueVec
      lp <- model$calculate(target)
      #lp <- model$calculate(targetAsScalar)
      if(lp == -Inf) return(-Inf)
      lp <- lp + model$calculate(calcNodesNoSelf)
      returnType(double())
      return(lp)
    },
    reset = function() {

      timesRan     <<- 0
      tries <<- 0

    }
  )
)

simpleCode<- nimbleCode({
  for(i in 1:100){
    gg[i] ~ dnorm(mean=0,sd=1)
  }
})
simpleModel <- nimbleModel(code=simpleCode, name="simp", constants=list(),
                           data=list(),
                           inits = list(gg=rep(0,100)))
simpleConf <- configureMCMC(simpleModel,monitors="gg",print = TRUE)
simpleConf$removeSampler("gg")
simpleConf$addSampler("gg[1:100]",type="sampler_latent_slice")
simpleConf$printSamplers()

                             resetFunctions = TRUE, showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

                         niter=5000,
                         #nburnin = 10000,
                         #thin=100,
                         nchains = 1,
                         progressBar = T
)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for posting and welcome to nimble.

I think the issue is that vectors in nimble should be indexed only with single brackets ('['), not double brackets ('[[').

You have a bunch of double-bracket indexing in this code piece

if( y_star[[j]] < y0[[j]]){
          a[[j]] <- max(a[[j]],y_star[[j]])
        } else {
          b[[j]] <- min(b[[j]],y_star[[j]])
        }

R lets you index a vector with either [ or [[, but nimble compiles only the [ syntax.

I made that change, and then code compiled, ran, and appears to be mixing.

Let us know further questions.

Perry

P.S. nimble didn't error-trap the issue very helpfully at all.  One strategy I can suggest is
options(error = recover)
then run the code generating the error (the compileNimble call in this case),
then go into the deepest level of the call stack (26 in this case, which is listed by the recover function),
then see what the variable 'code' contains, and in this case it was "y_star[[j]]", a hint that something is going on with this syntax.
And I'll file an issue for nicer error-trapping of this case.

> Dave, the error is coming from the cyclic dependence between elements of m[] and r[], in the following code (I've combined the two for-loops into a single loop, for clarity):

>     # Multinomial likelihood
>     for (t in 1:(2 * (nyears - 1))){

> Here, m[t, 1:nyears] depends on r[t].

Hi Rebecca,

Very glad to hear you worked it out.  I know that feeling of having something not work and then somehow work when someone else tries or suggests it because something else must have been changed while you were working on it.

Your ideas sound good.  A place where some serious effort has gone into reducing computational cost of augmented individuals is in nimbleSCR, as reported in Turek et al. (2021): https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.3385

In spatial capture-recapture (SCR), even when augmented individuals are "not in the model", their activity centers will be sampled by MCMC, and ensuing calculations of distances to all detectors and detection probabilities will be done, which are potentially quite costly (time-consuming).  A method to reduce this was to put those calculations into nimbleFunction(s) (which we did for other reasons anyway) and then also accept the indicator variable as an argument to the nimbleFunction(s).  Then the nimbleFunction(s) can know if an individual is not currently in the model and if so can skip to much faster processing steps, essentially skipping some costly calculations.  I hope that makes sense.

Good luck with it.

Perry

Hi Rebecca,

Very glad to hear you worked it out.  I know that feeling of having something not work and then somehow work when someone else tries or suggests it because something else must have been changed while you were working on it.

Your ideas sound good.  A place where some serious effort has gone into reducing computational cost of augmented individuals is in nimbleSCR, as reported in Turek et al. (2021): https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.3385

In spatial capture-recapture (SCR), even when augmented individuals are "not in the model", their activity centers will be sampled by MCMC, and ensuing calculations of distances to all detectors and detection probabilities will be done, which are potentially quite costly (time-consuming).  A method to reduce this was to put those calculations into nimbleFunction(s) (which we did for other reasons anyway) and then also accept the indicator variable as an argument to the nimbleFunction(s).  Then the nimbleFunction(s) can know if an individual is not currently in the model and if so can skip to much faster processing steps, essentially skipping some costly calculations.  I hope that makes sense.

Good luck with it.

Perry

> Thanks for this.  And thanks for the suggestion, Dan.

> I'm not easily grasping exactly what you need or what the problem is.  Could you try to pinpoint it more clearly (possibly referring to each line of code involved)?  One thing I'm not sure about is whether your code shows your workaround or shows what you would like to have work but doesn't work.
>
> If you need ages of augmented individuals to be latent states with valid initial values, would it work to provide their data entries as NA and their inits entries as valid values?  That is the usual approach.
>
> You might be saying that when w[i] is sampled to be a 1 (turning "on" an augmented individual), then you want an appropriate draw for the age.  It looks like the ages are stochastic.  Can you spell it out more?  I'm not sure whether you are seeing the error at (what we call) initialization, i.e. before the first MCMC iteration, or when a w[i] is sampled (or proposed by a sampler) to be a 1.
>
> A general comment: Data augmentation like this is a setup for inefficient MCMC.  That's because the MCMC will sample dimensions of the model relevant to augmented individuals even when they are not "in the model" (w[i] == 0).  An alternative is reversible jump MCMC customized to this kind of model.  We've experimented with that in simpler cases and it didn't help a lot, but it could help in other cases and just hasn't been something we've had time to do more with.  There are other ideas for sampling these kinds of models more effectively.  But anyway that's a side comment and does not address your problem.

> On Sat, Oct 15, 2022 at 6:12 PM 'Taylor, Rebecca L' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Dan,
> >
> > Thanks for that trick--it looks like it could be very useful for me down the road!  But I don't think it takes care of my current problem.
> >
> > Since my current model is age-structured, I need to pull out survival rates as phi[t, age] and recap rates as p[t, age]. But if age is specified as NA in the first time period (for the augmented individuals), I get an index-out-of-bounds error. If I specify a numeric age in the first time period for an augmented individual, then I don't think its age can't be overwritten in subsequent iterations. Thus, if K is the maximum age, I need K+1 separate groups of augmented individuals.
> >
> > Is there something I can do to separate out the first iteration to fix this? Perhaps assign everyone a non-age-dependent survival rate on the first iteration only? Or assign everyone an initial age in the first time period for the first iteration, but then let those initial ages be overwritten in subsequent iterations?
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > Rebecca
> >
> >
> > Rebecca Taylor
> > Research Statistician
> > Alaska Science Center
> > U. S. Geological Survey
> > (907) 786-7004
> >
> > Pronouns: She/her
> > Please note I sometimes send and answer email outside normal work hours.

> > From: nimble...@googlegroups.com <nimble...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Daniel Gibson <gib...@vt.edu>
> > Sent: Saturday, October 15, 2022 3:37 PM

> >
> >
> >
> >
> >  This email has been received from outside of DOI - Use caution before clicking on links, opening attachments, or responding.
> >
> >
> >
> > A few years ago, Richard Chandler posted a little trick on the HMEcology listserv that basically suggested that you could set spatial CMR likelihoods up in a way that only used the pseudo-individuals to inform the state process and completely exclude them from the observation process. This idea was expanded on by Alexandra Curtis to Jolly-Seber population models. I have no idea if this has entered the vetted ecological literature, but I messed around with the idea a bit, and it seemed pretty sound. So,although this doesn't change the number of pseudo-individuals you are using, it does change the extent to which they can bog down your model.
> >
> > I am just going to include an example code that I have used in the past that should be relatively similar to your code. I think this example was specifically written for JAGS, but I am not immediately seeing any nimble red flags.
> >
> >     ######################################
> >     # State Process
> >     ######################################
> >     for (i in 1:M){                                                   # Loop through real + psuedo individuals
> >      w[i] ~ dbern(psi)                                               # Latent inclusion state
> >      z[i,1] ~ dbern(eta[1])                                         # Entry into first occasion
> >
> >     for (t in 2:n.occasions) {
> >       q[i,t-1] <- 1 - z[i,t-1]                                                 # Have not entered yet
> >       mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1] + eta[t] * prod(q[i,1:(t-1)]) # Presence = survived since last + entered since last
> >       z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
> >     }
> >     }
> >
> >     ######################################
> >     # Observation Process
> >     ######################################
> >     for (i in 1:n.ch <https://gcc02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fn.ch%2F&data=05%...%40usgs.gov%7C130749f02b764f6e53e308dab76770cc%7C0693b5ba4b184d7b9341f32f400a5494%7C0%7C0%7C638023952208562687%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=kcUCeLc0ZOcoCVNXLLxhj1hVMcSfcqeXofj1EJxpnoM%3D&reserved=0>){                            # Loop through real individuals
> >       y[i,1] ~ dbern(z[i,1] * p[1] * w[i])     # Latent state * detection * latent inclusion
> >     for (t in 2:n.occasions){
> >      y[i,t] ~ dbern(z[i,t] * p[t] * w[i])        # Latent state * detection * latent inclusion
> >     }
> >     }
> >
> >     ######################################
> >     # Chandler trick
> >     ######################################
> >     for(i in (n.ch <https://gcc02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fn.ch%2F&data=05%...%40usgs.gov%7C130749f02b764f6e53e308dab76770cc%7C0693b5ba4b184d7b9341f32f400a5494%7C0%7C0%7C638023952208562687%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C3000%7C%7C%7C&sdata=kcUCeLc0ZOcoCVNXLLxhj1hVMcSfcqeXofj1EJxpnoM%3D&reserved=0>+1):M) {                                        # Loop through psuedo individuals
> >       pzo[i,1] <- 1 - (p[1] * z[i,1] * w[i])                      # probability of not being detected on first occasion
> >     for (t in 2:n.occasions){
> >       pzo[i,t] <- 1 - (p[t] * z[i,t] * w[i])                         # probability of not being detected on each other occasion
> >     }
> >       zeros[i] ~ dbern(1-prod(pzo[i,]))                         # probability of at being detected at least once (zeros = vector of 0's for each augmented individual)
> >     }
> >
> > #################
> >  This last bold-italicized part is the time saver. Instead of doing a bernoulli trial for i * t for these imaginary individuals, you just do it once for each psuedo-individual based on the probability of it being detected once per the duration of the study.
> >
> >
> > -Dan
> >
> > On Sat, Oct 15, 2022 at 4:52 PM 'Rebecca Taylor' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi all,
> > >
> > > I am working with an age-structured Jolly-Seber model (superpopulation parameterization with data augmentation.) Ages are observed without error for real individuals. The time 1 population is comprised of individuals of many ages. Entries in time 2 and beyond are by birth only. For augmented individuals, I would like to initialize all ages at “NA” so the ages can simply be determined by the code.
> > >
> > > That works fine if survival and recapture rates are not age-specific. However, if rates are age-specific, then the initialization fails because there is an “NA” being used as an index. For example, any individual in time t has a survival rate of phi[t, NA].
> > >
> > > I am able to work around this by assigning all augmented individuals an age in time 1. But that means I need many groups of augmented individuals—e.g., if there are 10 ages, there need to be 11 groups of augmented individuals (the extra group is for not yet born). And all groups of augmented individuals have to be pretty large, so I end up with a much larger augmented population and run time than I would like.
> > >
> > > Is there a way I can do something different on the first iteration to get around the initialization problem? Perhaps assign everyone a non-age-dependent survival rate on the first iteration only? Or assign everyone an initial age in the first time period for the first iteration, but then let those initial ages be overwritten in subsequent iterations?
> > >
> > > I hope this makes sense. I’ll copy code below. Thank you!!
> > >
> > > Rebecca
> > >
> > > code <- nimbleCode({
> > >   psi ~ dbeta(1,1)  # psi = inclusion parameter (is individual real or fake)
> > >   for (t in 1:K){
> > >     for(aa in 1:max.age){   # age 0 means not yet born
> > >       p[t,aa+1] ~ dbeta(1,1)# p[t,aa+1] = cap rate for time t, age aa; age 0 cap rate = 0
> > >     }
> > >   }
> > >   for (t in 1:(K-1)){
> > >     for(aa in 1:(max.age-1)){
> > >       phi[t,aa+1] ~ dbeta(1,1) # phi[t,aa+1] = surv rate for time t, age aa; age 0 surv rate = 0
> > >     }
> > >   }
> > >   beta[1:K] ~ ddirch(b[1:K])   # betas = unconditional entry probabilities
> > >   eta[1] <- beta[1]            # etas = corresponding conditional probabilities
> > >   for(k in 2:K){eta[k] <- beta[k]/(1-sum(beta[1:(k-1)]))}
> > >
> > >   # piAGE = age distribution of animals alive in the population at time 1
> > >   # piAGEuncond has an additional "age 0" which means "not yet born".
> > >   # Entries after time 1 are by birth only
> > >   piAGE[1:max.age] ~ ddirch(a[1:max.age])
> > >   piAGEuncond[1:(max.age+1)] <- c( (1-eta[1]), eta[1]*piAGE[1:max.age] )
> > >
> > >   # Likelihoods
> > >   for (i in 1:M){    # M = size of augmented population
> > >     w[i] ~ dbern(psi)# w[i] = indicator if individual i is real
> > >
> > >     # agePlusOne are time 1 age data + 1
> > >     agePlusOne[i] ~ dcat(piAGEuncond[1:(max.age+1)])
> > >     age[i,1] <- (agePlusOne[i]-1)
> > >
> > >     # state process
> > >     u[i,1] <- step(age[i,1]-.1)  # u[i,j] = indicator for alive
> > >     z[i,1] <- u[i,1]*w[i]
> > >
> > >     # Observation process
> > >     yprob_t1[i,1] <- z[i,1]*p[1,age[i,1]+1]
> > >     y[i,1] ~ dbern(yprob_t1[i,1] )
> > >
> > >     # avail[i,j] = indicator if not yet recruited from superpop to pop
> > >     avail[i,1] <- 1 - u[i,1]
> > >
> > >     for (t in 2:K){
> > >       # State process
> > >       uprob[i,t] <- u[i,t-1]*phi[t-1,age[i,t-1]+1]  + avail[i,t-1]*eta[t]
> > >       u[i,t] ~ dbern(uprob[i,t])
> > >       z[i,t] <- u[i,t]*w[i]
> > >
> > >       # Age process: grows older by one year after recruitment
> > >       age[i,t] <- age[i,t-1] + max(u[i,1:t])
> > >
> > >       # Observation process
> > >       yprob[i,t] <- z[i,t]*p[t,age[i,t]+1]
> > >       y[i,t] ~ dbern(yprob[i,t])
> > >
> > >       # avail[i,j] = indicator if not yet recruited from superpop to pop
> > >       avail[i,t] <- 1- max(u[i,1:t])
> > >     } #t
> > >   } #i
> > > })#END model

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks for explaining the issue and pointing out the computational inefficiencies.

I modified the code and it did work, however, I ended up having to pad the matrix object in for both rows and columns. It was giving me an error when I returned a 1x2 matrix for example.

conditional_MNV <- nimbleFunction(

  run = function(mu_vec = double(1), cov_mat = double(2), mu_vec_cond_pad = double(1)){

    mu_vec_cond <- numeric(length(mu_vec_cond_pad)-1, value = -999)
    mu_vec_cond[1:(length(mu_vec_cond_pad)-1)] <- mu_vec_cond_pad[1:(length(mu_vec_cond_pad)-1)]

    mat_size <- length(mu_vec)
    cond_vec_size <- length(mu_vec_cond)
    index_end <- mat_size-cond_vec_size

    #convert vectors to matrices
    mu_vec_mat <- matrix(0, nrow = mat_size, ncol = 1)
    mu_vec_mat[,1] <- mu_vec
    mu_vec_cond_mat <- matrix(0, nrow = cond_vec_size, ncol = 1)
    mu_vec_cond_mat[,1] <- mu_vec_cond

    #Inverse VCOV
    inv_cov_mat <- matrix(0, nrow = cond_vec_size, ncol = cond_vec_size)
    inv_cov_mat[1:cond_vec_size,1:cond_vec_size] <- inverse(cov_mat[(index_end+1):mat_size,(index_end+1):mat_size])

    resMatrix <- matrix(0, nrow = index_end+1, ncol = index_end+1) #padding row too
    resMatrix[1:index_end,1:index_end] <- cov_mat[1:index_end,1:index_end] - cov_mat[1:index_end,(index_end+1):mat_size]%*%inv_cov_mat[1:cond_vec_size,1:cond_vec_size]%*%cov_mat[(index_end+1):mat_size,1:index_end]
    resMatrix[1:index_end,index_end +1] <- mu_vec_mat[1:index_end,] + cov_mat[1:index_end,(index_end+1):mat_size]%*%inv_cov_mat[1:cond_vec_size,1:cond_vec_size]%*%(mu_vec_cond_mat-mu_vec_mat[(index_end+1):mat_size,])

    returnType(double(2))
    return(resMatrix)
  }
)

Thanks again,
Philip

On Thursday, 20 October 2022 at 16:57:57 UTC+1 pdevalpine wrote:
> Hi Philip,
>
> You can test the function and its compilation outside of a model.  I am guessing sd_diag was supposed to be sd_vec, so I've made that change.
>
> sd_vec <- c(.2,0.5,0.1)
> cov_mat <-diag(sd_vec)%*%R%*%diag(sd_vec)
>
> mu_vec <- c(5, 2,1)
> mu_condit_val <- 3
>
> conditional_MNV(mu_vec, cov_mat, mu_condit_val) # uncompiled: works
>
> C_conditional_MNV <- compileNimble(conditional_MNV) # compile it
> C_conditional_MNV(mu_vec, cov_mat, mu_condit_val) # compiled: works
>
> So the problem is how you are using it in a model.
>
> Unfortunately a friction point in nimble is that compilation supports true scalars, but R does not have true scalars (only length 1 vectors).  As a result, the single value mu_condit_val[1:1] is not passed as a vector successfully.  If you will always have a scalar here, declare it as double(0) instead of double(1).  Alternatively, if sometimes you. need a vector, you can pad it with an extra 0, which you can then not use within the conditional_MVN function.
>
> Also I would suggest a different strategy within conditional_MVN if computational efficiency is a concern.  Instead of repeating the step
> cov_mat[1:index_end,(index_end+1):mat_size]%*%inverse(cov_mat[(index_end+1):mat_size,(index_end+1):mat_size])
> you could do that once and re-use the result in both places where it's needed.
> Another strategy would be to do this calculation within the model (or as a separate user-defined function) and then have separate functions to obtain the conditional mean and conditional covariance, using this shared part of the calculation as input.
>
> HTH
> Perry
