messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have the attached code, which is written using the multivariate normal distribution; I would like to convert the code to be in univariate normal distribution using vectorization; in the multivariate normal distribution, the precision matrix is a diagonal matrix.

The code using multivariate normal:
N <- 64
S <- 64

mybeta <- c(2, 0, 0, 4, 8)
set.seed(1)
x1 <- rnorm(64);
x2 <- rnorm(64);
x3 <- rnorm(64);
x4 <- rnorm(64);
x5 <- rnorm(64);
y  <- cbind(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5) %*% mybeta + rnorm(64)
## replicate y 64 times to make a square matrix for easy implementation
y <- matrix(y, nrow = length(y), ncol = length(y), byrow = FALSE)

library(nimble)

Code <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:S) {
    y[1:N, i] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:N, i],  tau[1:N, 1:N, i])
    mu[1:N, i] <- b[i, 1] * x1[1:N] + b[i, 2] * x2[1:N] + b[i, 3] *
      x3[1:N] + b[i, 4] * x4[1:N] + b[i, 5] * x5[1:N]
    tau[1:N, 1:N, i] <- diag(psi[i] * exp(-Dist[1:N, i]/lambda))
    for (j in 1:5) {
      b[i, j] ~ dnorm(0, tau = tau_b[ind[j] + 1])
      ind[j] ~ dbern(gamma[j])
      tau_b[1] <- tau_b0
      tau_b[2] <- tau_b0 * c
      gamma[j] ~ dbeta(0.5, 0.5)
    }
    b0[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    psi[i] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
  }
  lambda ~ dunif(0, D)
})

netdist <- read.csv('country_dist.csv')
my_points <- matrix(c(netdist$Longitude,    # Create longitude/latitude matrix
                      netdist$Latitude),ncol=2)

colnames(my_points) <- c("longitude", "latitude")

my_points

library(rdist)

df <- my_points
# distance matrices
dist_mat <- pdist(df)
dist_1 <- pdist(df[, 1])
dist_2 <- pdist(df[, 2])
# product distance matrix
dist_prod <- product_metric(dist_1, dist_2)

netdist<- (dist_prod )
dist2 <- (netdist)

Data <- list(y = y, x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3, x4 = x4, x5 = x5,
                Dist = dist2)

Const <- list(S = S, N = N, D = 50, tau_b0 = 100, c = 0.0001)

Inits <- list(psi = rep(1, Const$S), ind = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0),
                 gamma = rep(0.5, 5), lambda = 10)

mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code =Code, data = Data, constants = Const,
                       inits = Inits, thin = 1, niter = 5000, nchains = 1, nburnin = 2000,
                       monitors = c("b", "psi", "lambda"), setSeed = TRUE)

library(coda)
pos_mcmc <- as.mcmc(mcmc.out)
par(mar=c(1,1,1,1))

plot(pos_mcmc[,1:5])

#######The univariate normal distribution

N <- 64
S <- 64

mybeta <- c(2, 0, 0, 4, 8)
set.seed(1)
x1 <- rnorm(64);
x2 <- rnorm(64);
x3 <- rnorm(64);
x4 <- rnorm(64);
x5 <- rnorm(64);
y  <- cbind(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5) %*% mybeta + rnorm(64)
y <- as.vector(y)
library(nimble)
dnorm_vec2 <- nimbleFunction( ## Define the distribution
  run = function(x = double(1), mean = double(1), sd = double(1), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- sum(dnorm(x, mean, sd, log = TRUE))
    if(log) return(logProb)
    else return(exp(logProb))
  })
registerDistributions('dnorm_vec2')

Code <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:S) {
    y[1:N] ~  dnorm_vec2(linpred[1:N,i], sigma[1:N,i])
    linpred[1:N,i] <-b[i, 1] * x1[1:N] + b[i, 2] * x2[1:N] + b[i, 3] * x3[1:N]+ b[i, 4] * x4[1:N]+ b[i, 5] * x5[1:N]
    tau[1:N,i] <- psi[i] * exp(-Dist[1:N, i]/lambda)

    sigma[1:N,i] <- 1/ tau[1:N,i]
    for (j in 1:5) {
      b[i, j] ~ dnorm(0, tau = tau_b[ind[j] + 1])
      ind[j] ~ dbern(gamma[j])
      tau_b[1] <- tau_b0
      tau_b[2] <- tau_b0 * c
      gamma[j] ~ dbeta(0.5, 0.5)
    }
    b0[i] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    psi[i] ~ dgamma(1, 1)
  }
  lambda ~ dunif(0, D)
})

netdist <- read.csv('country_dist.csv')
my_points <- matrix(c(netdist$Longitude,    # Create longitude/latitude matrix
                      netdist$Latitude),ncol=2)

colnames(my_points) <- c("longitude", "latitude")

my_points

# dist_mat <- pdist(my_points)

df <- my_points
# distance matrices
dist_mat <- pdist(df)
dist_1 <- pdist(df[, 1])
dist_2 <- pdist(df[, 2])
# product distance matrix
dist_prod <- product_metric(dist_1, dist_2)

netdist<- (dist_prod )
dist2 <- (netdist)

Data <- list(y = y, x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3, x4 = x4, x5 = x5,
                Dist = dist2)

Const <- list(S = S, N = N, D = 50, tau_b0 = 100, c = 0.0001)

Inits <- list(psi_y = rep(1,Const$S), ind = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0),
                 gamma = rep(0.5, 5), lambda = 10)

mcmc.out2 <- nimbleMCMC(code = Code, data = Data, constants = Const,
                        inits = Inits, thin = 1, niter = 5000, nchains = 1, nburnin = 2000,
                        monitors = c("b", "psi", "lambda"), setSeed = TRUE)

library(coda)
pos_mcmc2 <- as.mcmc(mcmc.out2)

## plot the first five parameter estimates
plot(pos_mcmc2[,1:5])

messages.subject: Re: missing data solution
messages.subject_clean: missing data solution
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for following up, Robin.

In nimble there is an alternative to the zeros trick.  (The zeros trick is a way to get an arbitrary log probability included in the model by having a fake "data" value that is zero, and declaring it to follow a Poisson.  The log probability of a zero in a Poisson is -lambda.  So by calculating whatever log probability you want and assigning it to lambda, it ends up included in the model's probability calculations.)

In nimble, you can do that arguably a bit more readably and elegantly with a user-defined distribution.  The need arises when one wants to calculate a value, say y, and then have it follow a distribution.  It can be done like this:

y <- [some calculation]
fake_datum ~ d_my_dist(y, arg2, arg3)

When that code is in a model, the log probability contribution will come from calling:
d_my_dist(fake_datum, y, arg2, arg3, log=TRUE)

so you can then write d_my_dist to simply ignore fake_datum and use y, arg2, and arg3 for whatever log probability calculation you want.

HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Suzy,

I am not sure why you replicate your vector y into a matrix and then use each column each time in a for loop. Given you are considering a multivariate normal distribution, this is not needed. In your code, you repeated declaring some nodes, like those inside the j loop within the i loop. This does not make sense in BUGS language. In addition, the way you specified the precision matrix for mnorm is not correct. The matrix you generated was not diagonal. Another issue is that the default parameter in dnorm is prec instead of sd. In your custom dnorm_vec2 function you intended to use sd but inside the code it's actually prec. I have fixed all these. In the code attached you will see the two methods match well. Please let me know if you have any questions.

Best wishes,
Wei

messages.body_plain:
Hi Wei,

Thank you for getting back to me.

The multivariate code is provided by the authors of the paper titled "Geographically Weighted Regression Analysis for Spatial Economics Data: a Bayesian Recourse."  which can be seen here https://ys-xue.github.io/Bayesian-GWR/
using the code provided by the authors for extensive data set is computationally expensive, so I am thinking of a way to convert the code to be in univaraite normal distributions.

In this algorithm, we are interested in finding the posterior for each parameter for each region i. The authors used y[1:N, i] ~ dmnorm(mu_y[1:N, i], prec = tau_y0[1:N, 1:N, i]) where the precision matrix is a diagonal matrix.

In my suggested algorithm I used dnorm_vec2 , I got the posterior for each parameter in each region, but the results from both models are too different.

I was also thinking maybe the issue is related to the vectorizations, where the vectorized one might need to run for more iterations to converge because the mvnormal approach might be blocking some of the parameters by default (the vectorized function wouldn't block by default). So I ran the suggested algorithm for more iterations, but it does not work.

Could you please advise in this regard?

Thanks

In addition, the way you specified the precision matrix for mnorm is not correct. The matrix you generated was not diagonal. Another issue is that the default parameter in dnorm is prec instead of sd. In your custom dnorm_vec2 function you intended to use sd but inside the code it's actually prec. I have fixed all these. messages.subject: Nimble for multiple dataset on same model
messages.subject_clean: Nimble for multiple dataset on same model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nimble experts,

I have to run some simulation datasets using the same model, and I am wondering if we can create a loop to make things easier or if we need to use compile_model$setData for specific datasets every time. Please see the code below, I appreciate any insights and suggestions.

Icar.model<-nimbleCode({

  for (i in 1:N){
    rw[i]~dbinom(pw[i],tn[i])

    logit(pw[i])<-betaw+u1[i]

    lb[i]~dbinom(pb[i],tn[i])

    logit(pb[i])<-betab+u2[i]

    prow[i]<-exp(betaw+u1[i])/(1+exp(betaw+u1[i]))
    prob[i]<-exp(betab+u2[i])/(1+exp(betab+u2[i]))

    index[i]<-prow[i]-prob[i]

  }

  u1[1:N]~dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:N], tau1, zero_mean = 1)
  u2[1:N]~dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:N], tau2, zero_mean = 1)

  betaw~dnorm(0,10000)
  betab~dnorm(0,10000)

  #tau~dgamma(1,0.01)
  tau1~dgamma(0.1,0.001)
  sigma2.tau1 <- 1/tau1
  tau2~dgamma(0.1,0.001)
  sigma2.tau2 <- 1/tau2
})

Inits1<-list(tau1=0.1,tau2=0.1, pw=rep(0.1, 159),pb=rep(0.1,159),
             betaw=1 , betab=1, u1=rep(0.1,159),u2=rep(0.1,159))

Model.icar<-nimbleModel(code=Icar.model, constants=constant,
                        data=list(rw=sim$w1,
                                  lb=sim$b1), inits=Inits1). ----sim$w1 indicates simulation dataset 1

CModel.icar<-compileNimble(Model.icar)
LCModel.icar<-configureMCMC(Model.icar,print=TRUE,enableWAIC=TRUE,
                            monitors=CModel.icar$getNodeNames(stochOnly=TRUE,
                                                        includeData=FALSE))

LCModel.icar$addMonitors(c("index"))
Model.icarMCMC<-buildMCMC(LCModel.icar)
CModel.icarMCMC<-compileNimble(Model.icarMCMC,project=Model.icar)
niter<-200000
set.seed(234546)
samples1.icar<-runMCMC(CModel.icarMCMC,niter=niter,nburnin=150000,nchains=1,thin=100)

CModel.icar$setData(list(rw=sim$w2,lb=sim$b2)) ----running simulation dataset 2
samples2.icar<-runMCMC(CModel.icarMCMC,niter=niter,nburnin=150000,nchains=1,thin=100)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bill,

Thanks for the question.

You can also change the data values by simple assignment:

CModel.icar$rw <- sim$w2
CModel.icar$b2 <- sim$b2

(In fact, the setData method is really most appropriate for an uncompiled model before creating an MCMC.  At that step, setData both assigns values and flags those nodes as data nodes.  The data flags are then used by configureMCMC and/or buildMCMC.  If you use setData later from the compiled model, as your code does, it will assign the data values, but it is too late to change which nodes are flagged as data, so that will not be done.  Therefore, you might as well simply assign values without calling setData.)

If your question is whether there is any way to not do a new MCMC run for each new dataset: No, you need a new MCMC run for each.

HTH.

Perry

> Are there some examples in the nimble manual?
>
> On Sat, Oct 29, 2022 at 4:26 AM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > Thanks for following up, Robin.
> >
> > In nimble there is an alternative to the zeros trick.  (The zeros trick is a way to get an arbitrary log probability included in the model by having a fake "data" value that is zero, and declaring it to follow a Poisson.  The log probability of a zero in a Poisson is -lambda.  So by calculating whatever log probability you want and assigning it to lambda, it ends up included in the model's probability calculations.)
> >
> > In nimble, you can do that arguably a bit more readably and elegantly with a user-defined distribution.  The need arises when one wants to calculate a value, say y, and then have it follow a distribution.  It can be done like this:
> >
> > y <- [some calculation]
> > fake_datum ~ d_my_dist(y, arg2, arg3)
> >
> > When that code is in a model, the log probability contribution will come from calling:
> > d_my_dist(fake_datum, y, arg2, arg3, log=TRUE)
> >
> > so you can then write d_my_dist to simply ignore fake_datum and use y, arg2, and arg3 for whatever log probability calculation you want.
> >
> > HTH
> > Perry
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Oct 28, 2022 at 12:09 PM Robin Russell <robin...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hello if anyone is interested, one solution to my very poorly worded question is in Walsh et al. 2018 and involves the zero's trick from the WinBUGs manual.  The code is in jags but can be converted to nimble.
